doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

chapter: Following the drum to New York
title: Village Gate salsa nights and carrying Frankie's drum
summary: Frankie takes him under his wing; he carries drums at Village Gate and Boys Harbor, which Rowe likens to older apprenticeships.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: He freaked out. He couldn’t move. He was paralyzed. He was paralyzed. He was paralyzed. And of course, you know, I get on the phone after that and I called Emile and I said, “Emile, you wouldn’t believe this.” And I told Emile, I was like, I met two of the guys already. Because Frankie was one and Frankie took me under his wing. Frankie took me under his wing. And Frankie started teaching me. Frankie said, “Look, I want you to come up, this is where I teach up here. I think it will be much better for you to come up here, and I was with Frankie all the — now I was carrying Frank — now in those days, in the 80s, right, you had salsa nights at the Village Gate. Monday night at the Village Gate in New York City anybody who was studying percussion or interested in this feel had to be present there because that was school. That’s where all the greats came through. Francisco Aguabella, Mongo Santamaria, Carlos Patato Valdez, Tito Puente, Celia Cruz, you know I mean all of the people, all of the people. Papo Pepin, I mean everybody came through there and played, and you had to be there. And Frankie used to work with all of them. So Frankie would give me his drum to carry so that I didn’t have to pay, I would come in, you know, carrying Frankie’s drum and Frankie playing with everybody. Man, listen, that was school. That was school. That’s what I came through. And then he was up at Boy’s Harbor, the same place like Chembo studied up at Boys’s Harbor and everything else, same thing. Because that was the place where all of us were gathering information and taking an academic study of Latin percussion altogether.

But that story about carrying someone else’s drums, that mentorship, I’m really happy to hear that. Because fellows that were playing and learning in the 40s and in the 30s, that’s what they did. Eddie Locke the drummer talked about carrying Joe Jones’ drums or something.
That was part of the school.
Yes, yes, yes. And I was fortunate. I mean guys don’t do that these days you know. Everybody’s on a different wavelength man. But for me, that was just an honor. It was an honor.
